title: 2yr beginner trader + 2mo beginner "AI coder" hooked Claude up to Robinhood's Agentic account. Be honest with me: what am I doing wrong?
author: small-phoenix
selftext:
Ok so context on me first cause I think it matters: I've been trading stocks casually for about 2 years, and I've been messing with AI/coding for like 2 months. So there is a solid chance I've done something dumb here, and I genuinely want people to tell me if so, not just be nice about it lol.

**What I did**

Robinhood has a new "Agentic" account type designed specifically for AI agents to trade in — it's separate from your main account, so it can't touch your regular money. I connected Claude (Anthropic's AI) to it and set it up to scan twice a day on market days and look for trade ideas.

The rules I gave it:

    1. Check current positions; flag anything up or down significantly since purchase.
    2. Check recent earnings (1-2 days back, large caps). Only flag an idea if a
       strong EPS beat is CONFIRMED by positive price action — a beat with a
       falling price is a red flag, not a buy.
    3. Run momentum scans: large caps ($5B+), healthy RSI (50-68), real volume,
       clear catalyst. Skip stocks already up huge on the day, sector-wide
       selloffs, and illiquid names.
    4. If there's a good opportunity: propose ONE trade (small fixed size) with
       ticker, reasoning, and price — and ask for approval. Never place an order
       without an explicit yes.
    5. If a position looks like it should be sold, propose that the same way.
    6. If nothing clears the bar: "no trade today." That's valid and common.

Ground rules I set for myself:

* Claude proposes, I approve. It can NOT place a trade on its own, ever.
* Small test money only — started with $200, \~$40 per position
* No "falling knives" — good earnings + price still dropping = skip
* "No trade" is fine and expected most days, not forcing anything

Here's the actual account (small on purpose while I test this out):

https://preview.redd.it/tkfz0hqn3ibh1.png?width=2936&format=png&auto=webp&s=1b5e2a1c3e1e00bb245988a53a3c06e83b7ee7e9

https://preview.redd.it/sfmqtb2r3ibh1.png?width=1952&format=png&auto=webp&s=267565f67ece2067cc0d2309c99f2df5918b264b

AVAV was the standout so far, up 19% on a confirmed earnings beat. Everything else is small gains, nothing crazy.

**What I actually want to know:**

* Are my screening rules missing something obvious?
* Is there a dumb mistake in how I'm approaching this that a more experienced person would catch immediately?
* Anything about risk management I should tighten up before I put more real money behind it?

Please don't go easy on me — I'd rather find out I'm doing something wrong now while it's $40 positions than later. Appreciate any feedback.

comments.author: medialantern
comments.body:
What you're doing wrong is thinking "AI" is some magic new thing that never existed before. It has, for years, and all that's changed today is somebody said "hey, what if instead of a million params we did a billion? screw the cost!"

Current-gen AI tools are **not thinking machines**. They are "stochastic" models that are non-deterministic, but based on how they work are designed to "drive to the center" of a given value set. That means two very important things:

1. You can ask it the same question, with the same inputs, and get two different answers out.  
2. They are designed to find the center of a solution set, not the edges. Outliers that could have been right/successful don't make the cut. They want the average-best solution.

These two factors already make them a bad choice for what you're trying to do. If you can put exactly the same inputs, conditions, rules, metrics, and everything else into a model and then ask it twice what you should do, if it says "buy" and another says "sell" which is right? There's an old quote "A man with one watch always knows what time it is. A man with two watches never knows what time it is."

But moreover, I'm guessing you're forgetting or not aware of how they're trained in the first place. Current-gen "AI" models are called LLMs because they're trained on **language**. I mean, these folks bought and destructively-scanned books (they literally cut them apart, scanned, OCR'd the pages, and then threw the books **in the trash**). You're asking a model trained on Harry Potter and vampire-fanfic to build a trading strategy. That's what's wrong. You're doing that thing, and Harry Potter wasn't much of a trader. That's your problem.

Don't get me wrong, these models can be a force-multiplier. They can do sentiment-analysis, pattern matching and identification, breadth-based searches, extrapolation, and lots of other things way faster and more broadly than you can. But at the end of the day you need to add something. You need to be the one defining why something should be bought or sold - and why. Harry Potter doesn't know how to trade equities.

replies.author: Foreskin_Mafia
replies.body: Not only that but the raw model will do more harm than good. Hallucinating
